P1.evidence: P1a hit and the only clean instance in this batch — the rep had spoken to the setter and reflected the handover back: 'so I had a chat with Derek that you talked with... Let me give about what you've been up to, bodybuilding, boxing, which I love', and later confirmed the recorded weight target ('Right now you're 84 kilos, right?' / 'And you want to hit 78'). The prospect visibly felt seen. P1d hit — the open question is asked and framed well: 'I would love to hear more detail. What is it that you're trying to achieve? And how, in detail, how can we actually help you with that?' P1b partial — two of the four frame elements (where you want to go, how we help); where you are now and what you need were not set out. P1c miss — no frame agreement sought.

P2.evidence: Strong, and the nutrition work is the best in the batch. P2g hit and genuinely investigative — the rep did not stop at the first answer. He asked for the daily intake, then 'Does the second meal, the dinner, is it big?', then observed 'You know what? It sounds like you're not eating a lot', then probed the gap with 'how about any weaknesses, you mentioned you have a sweet tooth', then narrowed it to 'so there's one biscuit a day?' That sequence located the actual discrepancy — hidden sugar in biscuits, coffee and protein shakes — in a diet that looked clean on paper. P2h hit — 'How about your sleep? How did you recover?' followed by 'You wake up rested?' P2e hit — 'Your routine right now, it's strictly like strength, like kind of a bodybuilding style, right?' produced the full weekly split. P2f hit — results explored properly, surfacing the central insight that twenty years of training built a 300 kg leg press alongside restricted movement. P2a partial — weight and target were known from the application and confirmed rather than asked; age and height never established. P2d partial — hip mobility was discussed at length but the prospect raised it; the rep never asked the injuries-and-limitations question and never followed up on the volunteered 'weak lower back, weak glutes, maybe a bit of knee pain' or on the reference to pulling something in his back. P2i partial — 'It looks like you got lots of energy' is an observation, not the question. P2b miss — his office-based job and international business were both volunteered. P2c miss — health conditions never asked.

P3.evidence: P3d hit and asked almost verbatim, which is what unlocked the phase: 'But I would ask you, what's the bigger why behind this? Why actually?' The prospect immediately separated the two levels himself — 'the small why is I enjoy training and I want to be in good shape. The big why is I've got two young children.' P3g hit — driven all the way through: children aged 8 and 4, training alongside them in ten years, refusing to be 'the old man at the gym that can't do anything' at 52 or 53, and the longevity frame of 40-year-olds who move like 70. The rep extended it into legacy by asking about the children and discussing what sport teaches them. P3b hit — mobility and strength both explicitly worked, including the prospect's own question about preserving strength. P3a and P3c partial — the specific goals (78 kg, abs, deep squatting) were established but volunteered rather than drawn out by the scripted questions. P3e and P3f partial — covered inside the bigger-why answer rather than asked. P3h miss — no reflect-back. The material was sitting there ('so this isn't really about six kilos, it's about being able to train with Amelia when she's eighteen — is that right?') and would have been the strongest close available; instead the rep summarised his own impression: 'I love the conversation. I feel that your mindset is where it's supposed to be.'

P4.evidence: The weakest of the discovery phases, and the miss is subtle because this prospect has no consistency problem to diagnose — he trains every day and enjoys it. But there is still a root cause and it was never systematically excavated. P4a/P4b partial — twenty years of weight training and its outcomes were established, but never framed as attempts that failed to deliver what he now wants. P4c miss — the obvious question, why twenty years of disciplined training has not produced functional capacity or mobility, was never asked. The rep asserted the answer instead ('regular strength training, like bodybuilding type, doesn't give you the functional strength'), to which the prospect agreed — 'I'm like a poster boy for it right now' — but the script credits asking. P4d/P4e partial and late — the prospect eventually named the gap himself at 00:44:37, well AFTER the price: 'the shift that I'm looking for is something that I weren't going to be able to do by myself for a number of reasons. Otherwise I would have already done it.' That sentence was the sale, and it arrived in response to an objection-handling question rather than in Phase 4 where it would have done its work. P4f miss — the information-isn't-the-problem frame never delivered.

P5.evidence: Not run at all — no part of it, at any point. The prospect supplied his own consequence material unprompted and it was strong: 'I've met 40-year-olds who move like they're 70... I want to ensure that the steps I'm taking today allow me to get to the latter, not the other way around', and 'I don't want to be the old man at the gym that can't do anything.' The rep agreed warmly and moved on. Not one of the four moves ran: no 'if nothing changes, what does this look like in two years?', no 'are you willing to settle for that?', no 'why not?', no line in the sand. This is the third call in the batch with no consequence frame, and here it plausibly decided the outcome: the prospect's only stated reason for not buying was the absence of urgency, and Phase 5 is the only part of the process that manufactures it.

P6.evidence: Run properly and in the right order. P6b hit — asked and answered before any price was named: 'when we figure out all the details, you're going to be fully committed to showing up and doing the work?' / 'Oh yeah, absolutely. I don't do things by halves, like, otherwise it's just a waste of everyone's time. So I don't play that game.' P6a hit — asked twice in effect, once at the commitment stage and again during the objection sequence: 'And do you feel like you can get to your goals with, with this?', which produced the most valuable sentence of the call about not being able to make the shift alone. P6c hit — the rep secured the yes before moving to the investment. Sequencing note: as with every call in this batch, the three pillars were presented before the commitment check rather than after it, though here the pillar presentation also served to answer three genuine mechanics questions the prospect needed resolved before he could commit to anything.

P11.evidence: Payment and onboarding were unreachable — the prospect took a considered 24-hour decision window and the rep accepted it. Scored N/A. The handover itself was handled well: the rep established WhatsApp as the channel, sent a message during the call and had receipt confirmed ('I've just received that'), pinned the timing ('I'll drop you a note probably similar time tomorrow') and pre-cleared the onboarding route ('then I can message to someone within our team to get you onboarded'). What was missing was any mechanism to hold the decision — no deposit, no start date, no reason the answer had to come inside 24 hours other than the prospect's own courtesy, and the rep travelling from the next day.

objection_plays.detail: Four of seven moves, and the sequencing was right. The isolation ran first and well — 'let's put finances aside. Like does this kind of check all the boxes for you?' — followed by the belief question ('do you feel like you can get to your goals with this?'), a check for anything hidden ('apart from the finances is there anything else'), and the what's-stopping-you move ('So what's stopping you to actually start now?'). Missing and consequential: 'thinking isn't the problem, deciding is' was never said, on the one call in this batch where the prospect had just explicitly described his decision-making process as a deliberate multi-step routine; 'the way you've been approaching this brought you here — when do you make a different decision?' was never said; and 'that man you want to be — how does HE decide right now?' was never said, despite the rep having built a strong ten-years-from-now identity frame twenty minutes earlier. The rep substituted 'I thought you are committed', a guilt variant not in the playbook, and the prospect corrected it precisely: 'the commitment is not into training. I'm already training. The commitment is to shifting to what we've discussed.'

Correctly judged and correctly truncated. The rep asked the direct question rather than running the full interrogation — 'so is this 6k, like, and be honest, like, yeah, I'm a grown man so I can take a hit, is this 6k within your budget, within your ballpark?' — and got an unambiguous answer: '6k is within my budget.' Skipping cash on hand, monthly surplus, credit cards, available credit and investments was the right call for this prospect and should not be scored as a failure; the play's financial-picture sequence is designed for buyers who cannot pay, and this one plainly can. The genuine miss inside OC is different: the prospect immediately benchmarked against a UK personal trainer and placed the price 'at the top end of that', and that comparison was never answered.

The doubt was about competence with an unfamiliar modality rather than about outcome — 'have I got the right form to be able to doing this properly?... the biggest question was actually, am I doing it properly?' The rep handled it well but not with the OE play: he deferred it deliberately, then answered it structurally with the record-and-review video feedback loop, and the prospect confirmed resolution ('It covers my question from earlier'). Scored partial because the objection was resolved through product mechanics rather than through any scripted move, which was the appropriate choice here. A related doubt — whether replacing bodybuilding with kettlebells would cost him twenty years of accumulated strength — was answered with reassurance only ('So you're going to be good, believe me') and no evidence, immediately after the rep suggested starting at 16 kg to a man who leg presses 300 kg.
No spouse or third-party consult raised at any point; the decision is explicitly his own.
No timing objection from the prospect. The only scheduling friction came from the rep's own vacation and the prospect's travel the following day.

PROCESS GAP, NOT A REP FAILURE — the setter pre-quoted a price range. 'I asked him how much is going to be, he goes, it's between 1 and 6, but he goes, the next call will tell you more. So it's come out at 6.' The prospect therefore arrived anchored to a range whose floor is one sixth of the real price, and experienced $6,000 as the worst case rather than as the price. There is no play for repairing a bad setter anchor, and the closer did not attempt one — he neither acknowledged the range, nor explained why the number is what it is, nor reframed it. This is a setter-process defect that lands entirely on the closer and it needs fixing upstream.

SCRIPT GAP — a qualified buyer with no objection who simply will not decide in the room. This prospect confirmed fit, confirmed belief, confirmed budget and confirmed commitment, then declined to sign because deliberation is how he operates: 'Even if it was two grand, I think that's not the point... I wouldn't just be impulsively just saying yes.' Every play in the book assumes a concealed objection to be surfaced. There is nothing for the case where there genuinely isn't one — no deposit to hold a place, no start-date mechanism, no cohort, no expiry. The rep had no tool other than to accept a 24-hour promise and hope.

SCRIPT GAP — the in-person personal trainer benchmark. Third instance in this batch of a cheaper-alternative anchor going unanswered (after Simple and Sinister on the smanian call and a $500/month coach on the Eddy call). Here it is sharper because the prospect did the arithmetic out loud and reached 'it's at the top end of that'. He then supplied the rebuttal himself — 'But also, this is something different, right? If I was going to just pay for a personal trainer, I would have done it' — which is precisely the argument the playbook should be arming reps with rather than relying on buyers to make unprompted.

notes: Technically the most complete call in the batch on discovery: the only genuine P1a in the set, the best nutrition probing anywhere in the corpus sample, the bigger-why question asked verbatim, and a commitment check run properly before price. And it still did not close, for one identifiable reason: Phase 5 was never run. This prospect confirmed fit, belief, budget and commitment, and then declined to decide because nothing in the call gave him a reason not to wait — he even volunteered his own consequence material about 40-year-olds who move like 70, and the rep agreed with it instead of turning it into a cost of inaction. Three actions. (1) Escalate the setter anchor immediately: 'it's between 1 and 6' primes prospects for a price that is one sixth of the real one and hands the closer a range to defend instead of a number to justify. (2) Run P5 on optimizers — a prospect with no problem needs a manufactured deadline more than anyone, not less. (3) Arm reps with an answer to the personal-trainer comparison; three prospects in this batch have now anchored to a cheaper alternative and no rep has rebutted one.
